doc.title: Harold Ousley interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Playing blues in Chicago and learning keys at sessions
summary: Ousley recalls the Club 409 blues scene, working with Sunnyland Slim, Memphis Slim and Roosevelt Sykes, and the demands and generosity of Chicago sessions.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: Was there a separate blues scene also at that time? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-

Yeah. There was a club on 47th Street. I think at the Club 409. The people like Muddy Water, Sunnyland Slim, used to work there. I’d go by there and hear everybody. In fact I worked with Sunnyland and Memphis Slim, Roosevelt Sykes. Because in Chicago a lot of times if musicians wanted to work regular you had to work with blues groups, you know what I mean. So I got the opportunity, which was very good, because you add to your repertoire and your ability. And of course the blues is one of the centerpieces of the music. And the thing about the blues is everybody knows about the blues. Because if you live you’ve had the blues at some time and we can appreciate it, plus the blues is a music that can help you feel better, you can get rid of — it’s therapeutic you know. So it’s really one of the staple pieces and it’s important to be able to appreciate it and get into it.
Good statement. Probably you ran into circumstances playing in some new keys I would imagine, if you started playing with guitar players?

Oh yeah. Well during this time in Chicago there were musicians there who, when you go to a session, they would go through the keys. Especially if they stayed home and practiced and this was their thing. I remember there was a piano player there and he played saxophone and piano. And he liked to play up here. When he got on the bandstand, you had to be ready to play up here in whatever key he played in. So it was a place where you know if you went to a session you had to really prepare. And if you didn’t, you know you’d have to go home in the woodshed. So in that sense it was important to do. But then there was a lot of love too. A musician would say, a lot of times, you know if they saw you were struggling they would come and say well you should play big, play through all the keys, learn all the tunes or whatever. So it was very helpful. So there was some love there as well as competition.
